extraction.name: MathQA: Towards Interpretable Math Word Problem Solving with Operation-Based Formalisms
extraction.description: A large-scale dataset of 37,200 English multiple-choice math word problems covering multiple math domain categories, annotated with fully-specified operational programs (operation-based formalisms) to improve model performance and interpretability. The dataset is derived from the AQuA dataset.
extraction.creator: Aida Amini, Saadia Gabriel, Shanchuan Lin, Rik Koncel-Kedziorski, Yejin Choi, Hannaneh Hajishirzi
extraction.publisher: University of Washington, Allen Institute for AI
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset was constructed by taking problems from the AQuA dataset and annotating them with formal operation programs using crowd-sourcing. The process involved categorizing problems into math domains, pruning the search space of operations, and using a dynamic annotation platform to guide annotators in selecting operations and arguments. Quality control was enforced through accuracy thresholds and validation by multiple validators.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The AQuA dataset (Ling et al., 2017), which contains over 100K GRE- and GMAT-level math word problems.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Problems from AQuA were categorized into math domains using term frequencies. Noisy problems (unsolvable, duplicates, non-numeric, requiring brute-force) were removed. Annotations were expanded for similar problems by replacing numeric values with generic numbers and using Levenshtein distance for similarity matching.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Problems were categorized into math domains (Geometry, Physics, Probability, Gain-Loss, General, Other) to prune the search space of possible operations. Noisy data from the source AQuA dataset, including problems with incorrect solutions, unsolvable problems, and incomplete rationales, were filtered out.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Crowd workers annotated problems using a dynamic annotation platform. Annotators selected operations from a category-specific list and valid arguments (numbers from the problem, constants, or previous calculations). The platform provided math knowledge hints, iteratively calculated intermediate results, and enforced quality control by requiring annotators to maintain an accuracy threshold on test questions. Validation required at least 2 out of 3 validators to rank the program as valid.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Expert evaluation of 500 problems showed 92% validity. There was 87% agreement between expert validation and crowd sourcing validation. The alignment validation accuracy was 94.64% across categories.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset aims to improve the interpretability of neural math problem solvers and reduce the influence of statistical bias in datasets like AQuA. It poses new challenges for future research as model performance is still significantly lower than human performance.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset contains noise from the source AQuA dataset, including near-duplicates and problems with incorrect solutions or incomplete rationales. The categorization strategy using n-gram frequencies can be noisy (e.g., words like 'square' or 'cube' might refer to geometry or exponential operations).
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset does not cover high-order polynomials or problems where solutions are entirely non-numeric. It lacks support for sequence problems and factorization operations. The categorization strategy is limited by using only one mathematical interpretation for domain-specific n-grams. Model performance is still lower than human performance.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, Testing, Validation, and Fine Tuning of neural sequence-to-program models for math word problem solving. It is also used for evaluating model interpretability and logical reasoning capabilities.
